data.title: Metabolic-Reproductive Hormone Integration
data.mission: Enable coordinated integration of insulin and metabolic signalling with reproductive hormone balance.
data.summary: Metabolic signals can influence reproductive hormone production, rather than merely accompanying it. Insulin experiments in ovarian cells identify one direct connection. In women with PCOS, a low-glycaemic-index dietary pattern improved selected insulin-sensitivity and menstrual-cycle readouts compared with a healthy comparison diet. This supports a contextual dietary-practice route, not a requirement for one isolated food or nutrient. The endocrine response depends on the population and treatment context; improved cyclicity does not establish a uniform change in every reproductive hormone.
data.dose_sensitivity: Pattern-based glycaemic stability with fermentable substrate support

phenome_relationships.rationale: Insulin sensitivity and metabolic stability interact with reproductive hormone regulation; this PM should be framed as metabolic-endocrine integration rather than a direct ADHD treatment claim.
Metabolic volatility may indirectly influence affective regulation through neuroendocrine and reproductive hormone coupling.
Insulin-linked metabolic signalling and gut ecological context may modulate oestrogen-progesterone balance across feeding and stress cycles.

## BRS-X-Hormones-1-4 - Metabolic-Reproductive Hormone Integration ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Enable coordinated integration of insulin and metabolic signalling with reproductive hormone balance. ### Overview Metabolic signals can influence reproductive hormone production, rather than merely accompanying it. Insulin experiments in ovarian cells identify one direct connection. In women with PCOS, a low-glycaemic-index dietary pattern improved selected insulin-sensitivity and menstrual-cycle readouts compared with a healthy comparison diet. This supports a contextual dietary-practice route, not a requirement for one isolated food or nutrient. The endocrine response depends on the population and treatment context; improved cyclicity does not establish a uniform change in every reproductive hormone. Nestler et al. (1998) [[3]](#pm-ref-3); Marsh et al. (2010) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) - **Biological Relevance:** Insulin stimulated testosterone production through its receptor and an inositolglycan-sensitive signalling route. Nestler et al. (1998) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) - **Implementation Notes:** Use the bounded dietary-pattern relationship below; its context and limitations travel with the disclosure. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects - Insulin stimulated testosterone production through its receptor and an inositolglycan-sensitive signalling route. Nestler et al. (1998) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) - Completers showed better oral-test insulin sensitivity and menstrual cyclicity with low GI; reproductive hormone superiority was not established. Marsh et al. (2010) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) ## 3. Levers
No Direct or Derived Dietary Requirement is currently established.
No evidence-supported cofactors or substrates are currently established for this mechanism.
No mapping established.
- Low-GI dietary pattern in PCOS
No evidence-qualified Lifestyle Lever is currently established.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Insulin stimulated testosterone production through its receptor and an inositolglycan-sensitive signalling route. Nestler et al. (1998) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) **Mechanism boundary:** The dietary trial did not establish insulin mediation or superior reproductive hormone concentrations; broader reproductive and neural benefit is unestablished. ### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Human cell experiments establish an insulin-to-steroid route. The dietary trial supports selected PCOS readouts, with attrition and treatment interaction limiting causal integration claims. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - None listed ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS-X(Hormones-FM1) — Reproductive Hormone Balance & Neurocognitive Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-fm1-reproductive-hormone-balance-and-neurocognitive-regulation) — Parent integration combines these child processes without establishing a new nutrient or outcome claim. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM1) — Oestrogen Signalling Stability](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm1-oestrogen-signalling-stability) — Assesses neural estrogen responses; intestinal recycling and circulating concentration are different endpoints. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM2) — Estrobolome Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm2-estrobolome-regulation) — Assesses microbial estrogen deconjugation; systemic recycling requires its own endpoint evidence. - [BRS1(FM1) — Monoaminergic Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function) — Candidate contextual connection retained for review; an exposure-specific resource or signalling relationship is not yet characterised. - [BRS5-FM2-PM5 — SCFA Production & Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm2/brs5-fm2-pm5-scfa-production-and-signalling) — Candidate contextual connection retained for review; an exposure-specific resource or signalling relationship is not yet characterised. - [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity & Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface) — Candidate contextual connection retained for review; an exposure-specific resource or signalling relationship is not yet characterised. - [BRS6(FM1) — Glycaemic–Insulin Stability & Cognitive Energy Availability](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm1/brs6-fm1-glycaemic-insulin-stability-and-cognitive-energy-availability) — Insulin availability provides metabolic context for steroid synthesis; a clinical response requires the population-specific evidence retained here. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM1) — Oestrogen Signalling Stability](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm1-oestrogen-signalling-stability) — Assesses neural estrogen responses; intestinal recycling and circulating concentration are different endpoints. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM2) — Estrobolome Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm2-estrobolome-regulation) — Assesses microbial estrogen deconjugation; systemic recycling requires its own endpoint evidence. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM3) — Progesterone-Supportive Microbial Metabolism](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm3-progesterone-supportive-microbial-metabolism) — Assesses microbial progestin production; endocrine stability is a separately unresolved claim. **Phenome assessment boundary:** Existing ratings and their original source records are retained pending outcome reassessment. title: Testosterone Signalling Stability
mission: Maintain androgen receptor signalling so motivation, stamina, and goal-directed effort remain well supported.
rationale: Serum testosterone after sleep or zinc manipulation is not a direct measure of androgen-receptor signalling stability. No food efficacy claim admitted.

data.title: Testosterone Signalling Stability
data.mission: Maintain androgen receptor signalling so motivation, stamina, and goal-directed effort remain well supported.
data.summary: Androgen signalling depends partly on the availability of hormones that activate its receptors. Nutritional and sleep conditions can influence this upstream supply, although hormone concentration is not a direct receptor-activity measurement. Small human studies found lower testosterone during zinc restriction and sleep restriction, with repletion findings confined to marginal zinc deficiency. These results support bounded supply and lifestyle relationships. They do not establish that extra zinc increases motivation or that manipulating testosterone is an appropriate goal for adequately nourished people.
data.dose_sensitivity: Pattern-based; androgen exposure context and life-stage matter

phenome_relationships.rationale: Testosterone signalling has been associated with motivation, effort, behavioural activation and goal-directed behaviour.
Low testosterone states are associated with reduced energy, fatigue and reduced mental stamina, but direct ADHD-specific evidence remains limited.
Androgen signalling may influence mood and emotional regulation through interactions with multiple neural systems.

a clinical response requires the population-specific evidence retained here. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS-X(Hormones-PM6) — Androgen-Microbiome Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/hormones/fm1/brs-x-hormones-pm6-androgen-microbiome-regulation) — Assesses intestinal androgen metabolism; microbial hormone conversion is not the same biological job. **Phenome assessment boundary:** Existing ratings and their original source records are retained pending outcome reassessment. The new mechanism and lever Findings do not validate or raise those ratings. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Each Phenome relationship has two independent ratings. They are not combined or averaged.

title: Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation
mission: Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on.
rationale: Established amino-acid provision retained historically. Aggregate indispensable-AA/protein identities, six missing individual EAA composition mappings and formulation/digestibility attribution prevent complete rapid food abstraction of this pool.

data.title: Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation
data.mission: Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on.
data.summary: Food protein supplies indispensable amino acids—the amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts—including phenylalanine and tryptophan. Phenylalanine can also be converted to tyrosine. After a protein meal, dietary phenylalanine appears in the circulation. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later signalling can use for dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. Protein that covers those amino acids is the supported dietary route.
data.dose_sensitivity: Not established as a neurotransmitter dose. Protein type, dose and age change how much dietary phenylalanine reaches the circulation. Extra protein is not shown to raise brain monoamines.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Coverage of the indispensable amino-acid set, including phenylalanine, that sets the circulating pool neurotransmitter pathways can draw on. Meals contribute measurable amino-acid composition; this is not a requirement that each meal provide complete coverage
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Protein-quality scoring and vegetarian-diet amino-acid coverage do not establish that increasing protein raises brain monoamine synthesis or improves attention or mood. The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted precursor/transport role, but this entry does not explicitly establish its dietary supply route. Clarification required; not defaulted to No.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Catecholamine precursor in the circulating pool this PM prioritises. Tyrosine is normally formed from indispensable phenylalanine and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid. Pool presence or dietary tyrosine is not evidence for increased brain dopamine or noradrenaline, LAT1 advantage, or clinical benefit. Absence of a phenylalanine atom is an evidence-scope decision, not a claim that phenylalanine is absent from the indispensable pool.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Pool presence of tryptophan is not evidence for increased brain serotonin, brain entry, or an attention or mood benefit.

The indispensable set includes phenylalanine; tyrosine is not an indispensable amino acid.

Absence of a phenylalanine atom is an evidence-scope decision, not a claim that phenylalanine is absent from the indispensable pool.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: Imbalance of LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance can constrain this mechanism’s governed circulating amino-acid pool.
established_links: This mechanism’s overview treats circulating pool sufficiency as independent of blood–brain-barrier transport.
Fernstrom 2013 locates LNAA competition at LAT1, which is the transport mechanism.
inferred_links: LAT1 imbalance would therefore reduce the circulating pool this PM governs.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: The named competitive state is brain-entry competition, not circulating-pool availability. That is a different process. Neither assessed arm is admitted as a mapping to the current KC1 definition.

kc_change_control_flags.proposition: Candidate PM↔KC1 mapping on the amino-acid quality arm. Shared IAA/protein-quality pool may constrain this PM; competitive LAT1 balance is not this PM's relationship. Input overlap with §4.1.1 is not a rejection criterion. Public §4.1.3 has no mapping. Dual-arm iKC remains KC-owned.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Meal protein supplies circulating phenylalanine, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later catecholamine and serotonin pathways can use. These studies do not measure attention.
Phenylalanine from dietary protein can be converted to tyrosine, the dopamine precursor. That supply is not a measurement of motivation or drive, and it is not dopaminergic signalling.
Tryptophan is an indispensable amino acid and the serotonin precursor. Coverage of that amino acid is not a measurement of emotional regulation, and serotonin signalling is a later step.

data.scientific_findings_intro: Dietary protein supplies the circulating precursor pool; food structure and source can alter delivery kinetics without proving superior neurotransmitter function. Curated reaction identity, whole-diet adequacy and experimental intervention findings are distinguished below.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Dietary protein and amino-acid availability
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human tracer studies establish dietary delivery. Cross-study source/dose comparisons and variable age results require qualified interpretation.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Dietary protein supplies phenylalanine to the human circulation, with delivery kinetics varying by the tested protein source, dose and meal context. The pooled age association is context-dependent, not proof that ageing uniformly impairs absorption or that greater availability increases brain neurotransmitters.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The pooled dairy corpus establishes dietary tracer appearance but is not 18 independent research-group replications. Independent human source comparisons support context-dependent plasma responses. An individual exercise study and the newer six-source crossover did not show a uniform age-related decrement; plasma profiles and dietary tracer appearance are not identical measurements.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mostly male dairy-tracer cohorts; between-study source/dose contrasts, nonrandomised age comparisons and different matrices limit generalisation. No brain transport, neurotransmitter or ADHD endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Gorissen et al. (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: dietary whey, casein or milk protein
evidence_considered.directional_finding: About half of dietary protein-derived phenylalanine appeared in the circulation over five hours. The fraction was lower for casein, higher with a larger dose, and slightly lower in older adults.

assessment.study: Pooled analysis of 18 randomised trials using intrinsically labelled whey, casein or milk protein.
assessment.population: 602 participants, mean age 53 years. The age comparison used 82 young adults and 83 older adults.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine entered the circulation. Protein type, dose and age changed the fraction that appeared.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Mean appearance 50% ± 14% over five hours. Casein 45% ± 11%, whey 57% ± 10%, milk 65% ± 13%. Older adults 45% ± 10% versus young adults 51% ± 14%.
assessment.evidence_summary: A protein meal delivers phenylalanine into the circulation, and the amount depends on the protein, the dose and age.
assessment.limitations: Phenylalanine appearance is not the full indispensable set, not tryptophan, and not a brain or clinical endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Non-animal protein-source crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 30 g protein as milk, mycoprotein, pea, lupin, spirulina or chlorella; five-hour sampling; at least seven-day washout.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.

assessment.study: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.population: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes.
assessment.result: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows.
assessment.evidence_summary: Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.
assessment.limitations: Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows. Independent of Maastricht pooled dairy corpus; age analyses and six visits within a person are not six independent replications.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2011): exercise before protein
evidence_considered.exposure_context: Resistance-type exercise before labelled protein versus rest; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.

assessment.study: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.population: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total.
assessment.result: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Source-specific endpoint and uncertainty: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.
assessment.limitations: Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence. NCT00557388 is part of Gorissen2020; no double-counting.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Diet-wide amino-acid adequacy does not require identical complete meals
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Retain nutritional adequacy, but separate whole-diet coverage from acute food-specific kinetics.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Varied adult diets can provide digestible indispensable amino acids without requiring every meal to supply the full set. This nutritional-adequacy proposition does not establish an optimal neurotransmitter dose or demonstrate that all plant and animal foods have identical postprandial responses.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Existing vegetarian-diet and DIAAS reviews support adequacy across a varied diet. New human source and faba-bean studies qualify single-food composition/digestibility; they do not contradict adequate mixed diets. The recent systematic requirement review concerns quantitative requirements, not neurotransmitter enhancement.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Requirement reviews are not direct tests of neurotransmitter response or every possible plant diet. Energy sufficiency, variety, age and clinical context remain relevant.

evidence_considered.label: Mariotti and Gardner (2019)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Adult vegetarian diets that include protein-rich plant foods can meet protein and amino-acid requirements. Amino-acid deficiency is described as overstated.

assessment.study: Review of protein and amino-acid intakes from vegetarian and vegan diets in Western adults.
assessment.population: Adults, including older adults, eating vegetarian or vegan diets. Children are discussed separately.
assessment.result: Protein-rich plant foods can achieve protein and amino-acid adequacy in adults.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No single intake-response estimate. The result is adequacy against requirements, not a change in brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary patterns can cover the indispensable amino acids this pool requires.
assessment.limitations: Requirement coverage is not a plasma time course and not a neurotransmitter outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Moughan and Lim (2024)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Protein quality is scored by digestible indispensable amino acids rather than by protein grams alone.

assessment.study: Review of the digestible indispensable amino acid score a decade after its introduction.
assessment.population: Not a new human trial. The score is applied to foods and diets.
assessment.result: Quality depends on digestible indispensable amino acids.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No neurotransmitter effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Coverage of those amino acids is the quality claim this mechanism can use.
assessment.limitations: A scoring review does not measure circulating or brain amino acids.

evidence_considered.label: Marsh et al. (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Varied plant-protein sources across the diet can cover indispensable amino acids without combining complementary proteins in each meal.

assessment.study: Review of protein in vegetarian diets.
assessment.population: People eating vegetarian diets.
assessment.result: Completeness can be reached across the day rather than inside every meal.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No meal-level neurotransmitter measurement.
assessment.evidence_summary: Each meal does not have to supply the full indispensable set.
assessment.limitations: The review does not test brain precursor availability.

assessment.population: Systematic review of studies January 2000-May 2024; duplicate screening and risk-of-bias appraisal.

assessment.population: Healthy-human single-food tracer/intubation study, NCT05047757.
assessment.result: Individual amino-acid digestibility and limiting-amino-acid content differ; a single food score is not a whole-diet inadequacy diagnosis.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Phenylalanine-to-tyrosine conversion: biochemical provenance
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Established conversion chemistry; dietary admission and downstream catecholamine effects remain separate decisions.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH) converts L-phenylalanine to L-tyrosine. This endogenous route contributes to tyrosine supply but does not make tyrosine absent from foods or establish an independent requirement for extra dietary tyrosine.
scientific_findings.synthesis: UniProt P00439 and Rhea 20273 establish reaction identity; the Matthews human kinetic review remains linked for physiological context. No new intake-response or clinical conclusion is inferred.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Curated enzyme annotation does not quantify whole-body dietary contribution or human brain catecholamine flux. Do not automatically add every PAH cofactor as a PM1-specific dietary requirement.

evidence_considered.label: Matthews (2007)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine in humans. Tyrosine is normally dispensable and can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine availability is limited.

assessment.study: Overview of human phenylalanine and tyrosine tracer kinetics.
assessment.population: Human tracer studies in people with ordinary hydroxylation and in disorders that block it.
assessment.result: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine. The conversion depends on phenylalanine availability.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Kinetic rates are reviewed. No dietary dose for a brain catecholamine change is given.
assessment.evidence_summary: Dietary phenylalanine can supply tyrosine through a conversion that has been measured in humans.
assessment.limitations: Conversion kinetics are not brain dopamine or noradrenaline synthesis.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Downstream precursor identity is not a dietary efficacy result
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve precursor identity and the downstream PM2-PM5 boundary.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply the precursor pathways for catecholamines and serotonin, respectively. Their biochemical identity does not demonstrate that additional meal protein improves brain transmitter synthesis, attention, mood or reward.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Retain Aquili and existing precursor evidence as biochemical/contextual support, not evidence that ordinary dietary coverage reproduces depletion or pharmacological supplementation experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Transport competition, regional synthesis, release and clinical outcomes require their own evidence. No score is inherited from this elementary relationship.

evidence_considered.label: Aquili (2020)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: narrative review of depletion and supplementation studies
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tryptophan is named as the serotonin precursor and tyrosine as the dopamine precursor. The reviewed behavioural effects come from depletion and supplementation, not from meal-protein coverage.

assessment.study: Narrative review of tryptophan and tyrosine in executive function and reward.
assessment.population: The behavioural studies are mostly acute depletion or supplementation experiments.
assessment.result: The precursor relationship is stated. Cognitive effects in the review are not effects of this dietary pool.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No effect size for meal protein on brain transmitters.
assessment.evidence_summary: The precursor names are supported. The cognitive conclusions are not a result for this mechanism.
assessment.limitations: Depletion and isolated supplements are not indispensable-amino-acid coverage.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Food texture and amino-acid appearance
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover study of ten older men, 135 g minced beef produced greater six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance than the same quantity of steak. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably between preparations.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Texture affected source-specific tracer delivery, not every circulating or functional outcome.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The matched-food crossover supports a preparation effect on dietary tracer appearance. Null total-concentration and muscle outcomes prevent a generic better-protein or neurotransmitter interpretation. The thesis and publication describe one dataset.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

evidence_considered.label: Pennings et al. (2013): minced beef versus steak
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 135 g intrinsically labelled lean beef, same cut, minced patty versus steak; six-hour tracer follow-up.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.

assessment.study: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.population: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart.
assessment.result: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: minced 61% ± 3% versus steak 49% ± 3% (means ± SEM), P < 0.01; 12 percentage-point difference. No paired confidence interval calculated or inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably.
assessment.limitations: Small single trial; mean estimates and standard errors available, paired effect interval not extracted; no equivalence claim for null outcomes. Single empirical dataset; thesis and journal article are the same experiment, not replications.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Extrusion altered early amino-acid kinetics, not demonstrated total loss
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In a randomised crossover of nine healthy young adults, the tested high-moisture-extruded mycoprotein/pea blend delayed selected early plasma amino-acid responses relative to the dry blend. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different; the study does not establish poorer overall nutrition for all meat alternatives.
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Preserve both temporal differences and the null integrated endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Scope is circulating provision and the exact measured endpoint, not brain entry, neurotransmitter efficacy or a clinical recommendation.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human beverage experiment and in-vitro analyses address different endpoints. Selected phenylalanine/tyrosine peaks changed, while grouped integrated responses were statistically inconclusive. Composition, matrix and sampling constrain interpretation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Single small trial, no dietary tracer, numerous secondary endpoints and laboratory reconstituted products. Not proof of equal total absorption or a reason to avoid all processed plant foods.

evidence_considered.label: High-moisture extrusion crossover (2024)
evidence_considered.exposure_context: 25 g protein, 39% mycoprotein/61% pea; extruded versus dry-milled blend in drinks; five-hour samples.
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.

assessment.study: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation.
assessment.population: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation.
assessment.result: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Phenylalanine peak: dry blend 72 ± 3 versus extruded 58 ± 3 micromol/L, P=0.020; time to peak 32 ± 4 versus 83 ± 20 minutes, P=0.037 (means ± SEM). Total five-hour grouped amino-acid iAUC: no statistically significant difference; no equivalence bounds inferred.
assessment.evidence_summary: Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different.
assessment.limitations: Small single dataset; no tracer, many endpoints, uncertainty on paired differences; laboratory reconstituted products not every commercial meat alternative. Distinct study but same Exeter programme as nonanimal2024; not an independent replication of its six-source comparison.

evidence_dependency: Shared sources with PM1-F1 and PM1-F2 are reused for distinct propositions, not independent replication. Pooled studies, thesis chapters and journal reports may overlap.

decision.applicability_proposition: This mechanism governs the shared indispensable-amino-acid quality and availability pool.
established_links: Meal-level protein quantity, quality and distribution set the circulating indispensable-amino-acid pool this PM governs (PM1 mission and overview).
Mariotti 2019 and Moughan/DIAAS-type scoring describe IAA adequacy of that pool.
inferred_links: Incomplete pool quality would also raise brain monoamines or treat ADHD.
decision.rationale: Reassessed after user review: indispensable-amino-acid provision is already recorded in PM1-DIT-1 and does not establish an additional constraint. The canonical KC1 defines monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive transport, which is outside this PM's circulating-pool provision boundary. The prior quality-arm admission used the historical KC scope and is superseded; its evidence remains on the dietary atoms and this assessment.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Superseded scope: this proposition concerns the former broad indispensable-amino-acid quality arm. Current BRS1 KC1 is the monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive pool. Archiving does not reject general protein-quality biology or alter the separately assessed competitive/supply decisions.

pending_actions.action: PM1 review: adjudicate dietary tyrosine contribution separately from indispensability; preserve existing Unset admission pending approval.
Register an immutable SOP identity and reconcile strategy roll-up only if the proposed preparation relationship is approved. No food-strategy ID or food mapping invented.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Dominant
evidence_qualification.rationale: Retain the Diet-Dominant qualification for experimentally demonstrated dietary precursor provision, without a superiority claim.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: Human dietary tracer appearance and source-specific plasma profiles are not brain neurotransmitter or ADHD outcomes.

routes.intervention_effect: Dietary protein ingestion delivers labelled phenylalanine, with source and dose contrasts in human studies.
routes.context: Human controlled feeding/tracer experiments; mainly healthy adults.
routes.limitations: Meal source, dose, age and matrix constrain generalisation; adequacy is not enhancement.

routes.intervention_effect: Matched mincing-versus-steak changed six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance.
routes.context: Ten older men; same-cut beef crossover.
routes.limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Dietary Requirements remains the principal supply route: feeding interventions directly deliver the indispensable precursor pool across relevant protein sources. The preparation experiment remains evidence, not a selected or registered SOP pending exact-scope adjudication.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: No head-to-head superiority over all lifestyle or optimisation routes is established. Prominence concerns the mission-specific supply process; it is not a nutrient-benefit ranking.

assessments.relevance: The PM mission is dietary delivery to the circulating amino-acid pool.
assessments.directness: Human labelled dietary-protein experiments measure this supply rather than infer it from food content.
assessments.extent: Repeated feeding experiments show substantial dietary tracer appearance, qualified by five/six-hour windows, source, dose and population. No universal optimum or brain effect.

import ScientificFinding from '@site/src/components/ScientificFinding';

## BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation (Neurotransmitter Protein Requirements) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Ensure meal-level protein supply delivers the amino-acid foundation neurotransmitter pathways depend on. **Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Dominant
- Indispensable amino-acid supply - Tryptophan
- Tyrosine
No mapping established.
### Overview Food protein supplies indispensable amino acids—the amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts—including phenylalanine and tryptophan. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Phenylalanine can also be converted to tyrosine. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) After a protein meal, dietary phenylalanine appears in the circulation. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later signalling can use for dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Protein that covers those amino acids is the supported dietary route. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) - **Benefits:** These amino acids, including tyrosine made from phenylalanine, are how meal protein supplies the pool that dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin pathways draw on. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) That capacity is not evidence that extra protein improves attention or mood. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) - **Implementation Notes:** Indispensable amino-acid supply and tryptophan are the dietary requirements; food protein supplies these amino acids. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, so it is not classed as an indispensable amino acid. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) No neurotransmitter-targeted intake dose is established. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Each meal does not have to supply the full set. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) - **Biological Relevance:** Those amino acids still have to cross into the brain before they are used to make dopamine, noradrenaline or serotonin - see [PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ circulating indispensable amino-acid supply, including phenylalanine that can be converted to tyrosine ## 3. Intervention Levers
No PM-specific preparation protocol is currently selected. The qualified preparation experiment and pending intervention disposition remain in [PM1-F5](#pm1-f5) and its Evidence & Audit assessment.
No PM1-specific lifestyle intervention is selected after this assessment. Exercise, sleep and hydration findings remain available in Evidence & Audit; no demonstrated absence of broader benefit is implied.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH) contributes to endogenous tyrosine supply. [UniProt C1](#pm-curated-pah) and [Rhea C2](#pm-curated-rhea) establish reaction identity, not an independent dietary cofactor admission. ### Summary Later signalling can use tyrosine and tryptophan only after those amino acids are available in the circulation. A protein meal is what puts dietary phenylalanine there, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Brain entry and neurotransmitter synthesis come after that.
#### PM1-F1 Gorissen et al. (2020) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) pooled human trials of labelled whey, casein and milk protein. About half of the dietary phenylalanine appeared in the circulation over five hours. Casein delivered a smaller fraction than whey or milk, a larger dose delivered more, and the older subgroup showed a lower fraction appearing within the measurement window. That pooled association does not establish uniform age-related impairment. The measured endpoint is plasma phenylalanine, not brain dopamine, noradrenaline or serotonin. Supporting evidence: [PM1-F1](#pm1-f1). #### PM1-F2 Mariotti and Gardner (2019) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) found that adult vegetarian diets which include protein-rich plant foods can meet protein and amino-acid requirements. Moughan and Lim (2024) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) score protein quality by digestible indispensable amino acids, not by grams alone. Marsh et al. (2013) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) state that varied plant proteins across the diet can cover that set, so complementary proteins do not have to share every meal. Supporting evidence: [PM1-F2](#pm1-f2). #### PM1-F3 Matthews (2007) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) shows that humans convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, mainly in the liver. Tyrosine is normally dispensable because of that conversion, and it can become conditionally indispensable when phenylalanine is limited. The curated PAH reaction records identify this conversion without establishing a separate dietary tyrosine requirement. [UniProt C1](#pm-curated-pah); [Rhea C2](#pm-curated-rhea). Supporting evidence: [PM1-F3](#pm1-f3). #### PM1-F4 Aquili (2020) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) names tryptophan as the serotonin precursor and tyrosine as the dopamine precursor. Those names identify the amino acids in this pool. They do not show that a higher circulating supply raises brain serotonin or dopamine. Brain transport and downstream synthesis remain distinct from circulating provision. Supporting evidence: [PM1-F4](#pm1-f4). #### PM1-F5 Food structure can modify the time course and measured appearance of amino acids from an ingested protein source. In the matched beef-texture experiment, more dietary phenylalanine appeared in the circulation after mincing, but total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably. Dietary tracer appearance and total circulating concentration are different measurements; neither establishes greater brain precursor delivery. [Pennings et al.](#stage2-ref-pm1-pennings2013). Supporting evidence: [PM1-F5](#pm1-f5). The preparation SOP remains proposed, not admitted. #### PM1-F6 Processing can alter the temporal response without demonstrating a change in total measured exposure. The tested extruded mycoprotein/pea blend changed selected early plasma amino-acid responses, while the integrated five-hour grouped responses were not significantly different. Unlike the beef experiment, this study did not use a dietary tracer; the endpoints must not be treated as interchangeable or as proof of equal absorption. [Extrusion crossover](#stage2-ref-pm1-extrusion2024). Supporting evidence: [PM1-F6](#pm1-f6). No extrusion-related SOP is admitted. #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Competitive transport of amino acids across the blood–brain barrier is [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). Dopamine synthesis and signalling are [BRS1-FM1-PM3 — Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation). Noradrenaline signalling is [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation). Serotonin signalling is [BRS1-FM1-PM5 — Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation). #### (Integration within BRS1) This mechanism supplies the circulating pool at the start of [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function). Later mechanisms in that pathway draw on it. A shared key-constraint mapping is not established.
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Dietary protein supplies the circulating precursor pool; food structure and source can alter delivery kinetics without proving superior neurotransmitter function. Curated reaction identity, whole-diet adequacy and experimental intervention findings are distinguished below. {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F1:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Dietary protein and amino-acid availability

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F1:end */} {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F2:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Diet-wide amino-acid adequacy does not require identical complete meals

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F2:end */} {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F3:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Phenylalanine-to-tyrosine conversion: biochemical provenance

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F3:end */} {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F4:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Downstream precursor identity is not a dietary efficacy result

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F4:end */} {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F5:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Food texture and amino-acid appearance

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F5:end */} {/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F6:start */}

Mechanistic explanation: Extrusion altered early amino-acid kinetics, not demonstrated total loss

{/* scientific-lesson:PM1-F6:end */} ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM3 — Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM5 — Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) — Methylation uses methionine, another indispensable amino acid supplied by dietary protein. That is a shared amino-acid source, not a control this mechanism exerts on the methylation cycle. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — The tyrosine and tryptophan in this circulating pool still have to enter the brain. That entry is competitive transport, not this supply step. - [BRS1-FM1-PM3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — Dopamine synthesis uses tyrosine after brain entry, including tyrosine made from phenylalanine. This mechanism supplies that precursor. It does not carry out the synthesis. - [BRS1-FM1-PM4 - Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — Noradrenaline synthesis uses the same tyrosine after brain entry. This mechanism supplies the circulating precursor and does not regulate noradrenaline signalling. - [BRS1-FM1-PM5 - Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) — Serotonin synthesis uses tryptophan from this pool. This mechanism supplies that indispensable amino acid and does not carry out serotonin synthesis. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Each Phenome relationship has two independent ratings. They are not combined or averaged.

Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength

How direct and important is this biological mechanism expected to be to the Phenome within the BRAIN model?

Evidence Confidence

How strongly does the adjudicated evidence support this particular biology → Phenome relationship?

Focus / Attention Stability — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low–Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Meal protein supplies circulating phenylalanine, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later catecholamine and serotonin pathways can use. These studies do not measure attention.
Motivation / Drive — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low–Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Phenylalanine from dietary protein can be converted to tyrosine, the dopamine precursor. That supply is not a measurement of motivation or drive, and it is not dopaminergic signalling.
Emotional Regulation — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low - **Evidence Confidence:** Low - **Rationale:** Tryptophan is an indispensable amino acid and the serotonin precursor. Coverage of that amino acid is not a measurement of emotional regulation, and serotonin signalling is a later step.

title: LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation
mission: Influence competition for transport across the blood–brain barrier so neurotransmitter precursors can reach the brain after meals.
rationale: Historical meal carbohydrate/protein pattern admission conflicts with current section-specific eligibility. Plasma LNAA ratios are not measured brain LAT1 flux. Withhold this pattern from §3.1.1; no automatic SOP transfer.

data.title: LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation
data.mission: Influence competition for transport across the blood–brain barrier so neurotransmitter precursors can reach the brain after meals.
data.summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) helps control which amino acids can enter the brain. Tyrosine, tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) compete for this shared route. Human feeding experiments show that meal composition and protein source can alter their relative availability in blood. The response depends on the tested meal and sampling period, rather than a universal carbohydrate-to-protein rule. This transport step connects circulating precursor supply with downstream neurotransmitter pathways.
key_constraints: BRS1(KC1) - Amino Acid Quality & Competitive Balance
data.dose_sensitivity: Pattern target rather than single nutrient threshold; depends on protein/carbohydrate composition
data.scientific_findings_intro: LAT1 transport identity is separated from the experimental finding that meal composition changes plasma precursor ratios. Breakfast, evening-meal and protein-source results show why a between-meal difference must not be described as a universal rise above baseline. Plasma ratios do not directly measure brain transport or neurotransmitter production. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Competitive transport biology does not establish that eating more tyrosine increases brain tyrosine or catecholamine signalling.

dietary_lever_presentations.label: Meal carbohydrate-to-protein composition
dietary_lever_presentations.reader_description: The carbohydrate-to-protein composition of the tested breakfasts changed blood ratios among amino acids competing for brain entry. A between-meal contrast is not necessarily an increase above baseline: the recovered breakfast study found lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after its protein-rich meal. Responses differ with meal context and protein source. No best ratio or improvement in brain function is established.

pm_kc_relationships.dietary_input_note: Pool/constraint reference; constituent dietary supply is recorded separately.
pm_kc_relationships.pm_biological_role: This PM governs meal-level LAT1 competitive balance among large neutral amino acids.
pm_kc_relationships.evidence_limitation: Meal-level competitive precursor presentation is established; plasma ratios are not regional brain signalling outcomes. The former broad IAA-quality arm is archived as superseded scope and no KC nutrient list is inherited.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: This mechanism governs meal-level LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance.
established_links: Meal-level LNAA competition at LAT1 is the state this PM governs (PM2-F1, PM2-F2).
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: Type D is met in the governs mode. This does not decide the quality arm.

kc_change_control_flags.proposition: Whether BRS1(KC1) amino-acid quality constrains LAT1 competitive-transport capacity under Type D, without using assessment ownership as the reason.

phenome_relationships.rationale: Meal-level LNAA competition at LAT1 can shift plasma tyrosine and tryptophan ratios and, on review evidence, brain-entry bias {{cite:fernstrom_lnna_2013,ashley_breakfast_1985,wurtman_effects_2003}}. The attached meal studies do not measure attention or ADHD outcomes, and transport modulation cannot substitute for substrate sufficiency or downstream signalling.

The tested meals changed competitive plasma ratios; the recovered breakfast study did not show a tyrosine-ratio rise after protein {{cite:wurtman_effects_2003}}. This remains a translational mapping, not demonstrated motivation, drive or ADHD benefit.

Carbohydrate-rich versus protein-rich meals can change the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio {{cite:wurtman_effects_2003,ashley_breakfast_1985,fernstrom_lnna_2013}}. Plasma-ratio change is not serotonin signalling or an emotional-regulation benefit.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Shared LAT1 transport and precursor competition
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) carries competing amino acids as part of an exchanger complex. Blood ratios describe substrate presentation, not measured transport flux.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This establishes competitive transport biology. It does not show that eating more tyrosine or tryptophan increases brain monoamines or improves function.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Large neutral amino acids share competitive transport through LAT1 (SLC7A5) with the SLC3A2 heavy chain; plasma composition helps shape substrate availability but is not a direct measurement of net brain uptake.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Curated human SLC3A2 annotation and the deposited human LAT1 complex support transporter identity; the inherited Fernstrom review supplies the physiological competition context. Exchange, substrate affinity and cellular context qualify the simple plasma-ratio model. No numerical score is assigned merely for curated identity.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Curated transporter and structural records do not quantify an ordinary meal effect in the human brain. The plasma-ratio proxy is not the sole determinant of net flux. The original Finding ID and source history are retained.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary and plasma LNAA ratios influence LAT1-mediated brain uptake of tyrosine, tryptophan and related amino acids and can change precursor availability for neurotransmitter synthesis.

assessment.study: Narrative review of dietary LNAA effects on brain transport and neurochemistry.
assessment.population: Mixed human and experimental literature; not a single intervention sample.
assessment.result: Identified competitive LAT1 transport and plasma-ratio dependence as determinants of brain LNAA entry.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled meal-response effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes the shared-transporter rule that defines this PM.
assessment.limitations: Review synthesis; does not by itself demonstrate that ordinary meals change human brain monoamines or function.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Meal composition and protein source alter plasma precursor ratios
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Human feeding experiments demonstrate context-dependent plasma-ratio changes. A higher ratio after one meal than another is not necessarily an increase above baseline.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Retain the admitted meal-composition regulatory relationship at its plasma-ratio ceiling. Protein-source experiments qualify generalisation; they do not establish a best ratio, an additional nutrient requirement or a clinical protocol.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In the studied healthy adults, meal composition and tested protein sources can alter plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids; the direction and tyrosine response depend on the exposure and sampling context, without establishing increased human brain transport or neurotransmitter synthesis.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Breakfast contrasts and separate protein-source experiments support meal-responsive precursor ratios, but not one universal direction. The recovered Wurtman table shows lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after the protein-rich breakfast, not an increased tyrosine ratio. Evening-meal null results and a starch-control null constrain extrapolation. Brain uptake and downstream effects were not measured by those plasma experiments.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Small acute healthy-adult samples; different meals, ratio denominators and sampling windows; incomplete historical methods retrieval. No population-wide optimum or direct human brain-flux estimate. Evening null results limit generalisation but are not equivalence evidence.

evidence_considered.label: Ashley et al. (1985)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Breakfast carbohydrate-versus-protein composition changed the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio in healthy lean young men.

assessment.study: Controlled breakfast-composition experiment measuring plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids.
assessment.population: Healthy lean young men.
assessment.result: Breakfast composition altered the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Directional meal contrast; no general clinical effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows that a single ordinary breakfast can move the tryptophan competitive ratio.
assessment.limitations: Plasma ratio only; no brain transport, serotonin or functional measure; young male sample.

evidence_considered.label: Wurtman et al. (2003)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.

assessment.study: Random-order two-breakfast crossover; sampling through four hours, chromatographic amino-acid assays and mixed-model analysis with order and multiplicity considered.
assessment.population: Nine young adults entered; eight completed both conditions (six women, two men).
assessment.result: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Median between-breakfast contrast: 54% for tryptophan ratio and 28% for tyrosine ratio; these are not increases after protein. Carbohydrate-arm increases from baseline were not significant.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct plasma contrast, not brain transport.
assessment.limitations: One incomplete participant; visible meal differences and unreported concealment/assay blinding; residual uncertainty in magnitude and generalisation.

evidence_considered.label: Ashley et al. (1982)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.

assessment.study: Within-person evening meal comparison; author-posted results and figures recovered.
assessment.population: Eight healthy men.
assessment.result: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.
assessment.effect_magnitude: See source-specific results; no pooled effect or invented confidence interval.
assessment.evidence_summary: The unfortified evening meals did not significantly change the tryptophan ratio; tyrosine ratios were unchanged.
assessment.limitations: Different meals and time window from breakfast experiments; null significance does not establish equivalence.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom et al. (2013), protein-source experiment
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.

assessment.study: Four-visit feeding experiment, four-hour chromatographic sampling; full institutional manuscript examined.
assessment.population: Six fasting healthy men.
assessment.result: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.
assessment.effect_magnitude: See source-specific results; no pooled effect or invented confidence interval.
assessment.evidence_summary: Alpha-lactalbumin raised the tryptophan ratio, gluten and zein lowered it, and starch did not change it.
assessment.limitations: Order randomisation and blinding not established in the examined report; different denominator from Wurtman. Not a universal food ranking.

evidence_dependency: Ashley breakfast and evening reports share investigators; do not count them as independent-team replication. Wurtman breakfast and Fernstrom protein-source experiments are distinct datasets and teams, but test different protocols. Ratio denominators differ; no pooled effect is calculated. Markus protein studies are contextual corroboration, not extra replications of a carbohydrate-to-protein protocol.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma-ratio changes do not establish ordinary-meal functional benefit
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Enriched-protein studies include functional endpoints, but their exposures and populations differ from ordinary meals. Keep that evidence distinct from a demonstrated LAT1-mediated clinical effect.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Phenome mappings remain translational relationships. Precursor-loading or depletion cognition literature is a different exposure and must not be read as ordinary-meal LAT1 evidence.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: The ordinary-meal studies assessed here measured plasma amino-acid ratios, not brain transport or ADHD outcomes; findings from enriched-protein attention studies do not establish ordinary-meal efficacy.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The original meal studies do not measure functional outcomes. Markus et al. (2005) measured morning attention after an enriched-protein protocol, while a newer athlete trial reported null sleep/performance results. These contexts cannot validate a general ordinary-meal benefit or prove mediation by LAT1.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: This is an assessment-scope boundary, not a claim that functional evidence is absent from the entire literature. The enriched-protein trials are not ordinary-meal or ADHD trials; no equivalence or mediation is inferred.

evidence_considered.label: Aquili (2020)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Tryptophan and tyrosine can modulate executive function and reward processing in reviewed experimental designs, largely through acute depletion or loading rather than ordinary meals.

assessment.study: Narrative review of tryptophan and tyrosine in executive function and reward processing.
assessment.population: Mixed experimental and clinical literature; not an ordinary-meal LAT1 sample.
assessment.result: Precursor availability was linked to executive and reward measures in depletion and loading contexts.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled ordinary-meal or ADHD effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Shows that precursor-manipulation studies exist, but they are the wrong construct for this PM’s meal-level LAT1 claim.
assessment.limitations: Review-level; depletion and loading are not carbohydrate–protein meals and do not measure LAT1 transport.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Ashley et al. (1985)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Demonstrates that breakfast composition changes the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: No attention, emotional-regulation or ADHD outcome was measured.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Wurtman et al. (2003)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Demonstrates that ordinary high-carbohydrate and high-protein meals move plasma tryptophan and tyrosine ratios.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Plasma ratios are not Phenome or clinical endpoints.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Fernstrom (2013)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Frames why plasma LNAA ratios can change brain precursor entry.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Review of transport and neurochemistry, not a meal-to-Phenome or ADHD trial.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Plasma LNAA ratios are not monoamine dosing
scientific_findings.finding_summary: A change in the plasma tryptophan or tyrosine ratio is not a measurement of brain LAT1 flux, neurotransmitter synthesis or a functional outcome.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Read meal studies as plasma competitive-balance evidence. Do not restate them as serotonin, dopamine or ADHD effects.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Plasma large-neutral-amino-acid ratio change after a meal is not equivalent to measured brain transport, monoamine synthesis or a Phenome outcome.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The human meal papers report circulating amino-acid ratios. The transport review explains why those ratios matter at LAT1. Neither layer substitutes for a brain-transport, synthesis-flux or outcome measure.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: The constraint is interpretive. It does not deny that brain entry can follow plasma ratios; it denies treating the attached meal endpoints as if they were those later steps.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Dietary LNAA patterns can change brain precursor availability, but plasma ratio, brain uptake and neurotransmitter synthesis are separable steps.

assessment.study: Narrative review distinguishing plasma LNAA ratios, LAT1 transport and downstream neurochemistry.
assessment.population: Mixed mechanistic literature.
assessment.result: Supported competitive transport while keeping later neurochemical steps distinct.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No single-step effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Supplies the interpretive boundary between ratio change and monoamine effect.
assessment.limitations: Review-level; does not replace a human brain-transport experiment.

evidence_dependency: Fernstrom (2013) is also primary Evidence Considered in PM2-F1. Reuse here is interpretive, not an independent replication of the transport rule.

decision.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the shared indispensable-amino-acid quality pool can constrain this mechanism’s governed LAT1 competitive-transport capacity.
established_links: DIAAS and related scores measure digestible IAA adequacy for protein quality (FAO 2013; Mariotti 2019).
LAT1 competition depends on the relative plasma LNAA mix (Fernstrom 2013).
inferred_links: Incomplete IAA quality would therefore change the LNAA mix and constrain transport capacity.
decision.rationale: Assessment was completed. Quality-scoring evidence does not measure LAT1 competition. Fernstrom’s competitive effects assume LNAAs are present; they do not show that a DIAAS-type quality shortfall constrains transport capacity. Ownership on PM1 does not decide this arm.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Superseded scope: this proposition concerns the former broad indispensable-amino-acid quality arm. Current BRS1 KC1 is the monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive pool. Archiving does not reject general protein-quality biology or alter the separately assessed competitive/supply decisions.

decision.applicability_proposition: This mechanism governs meal-level LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance.
established_links: Meal-level LNAA competition at LAT1 is the state this PM governs (PM2-F1, PM2-F2).
decision.rationale: Type D is met in the governs mode. This does not decide the quality arm.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Metadata migration only: preserve the established governs/constrained-by interpretation as a typed Conditional constraint for FM summary derivation. No stronger scientific admission.

evidence_qualification.label: Diet-Dominant
evidence_qualification.rationale: Retain the accepted dietary state-regulation relationship, qualified to measured plasma-ratio effects.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: Acute plasma-ratio modulation in studied healthy adults, not demonstrated optimisation of human brain transport or function.

routes.intervention_effect: Tested meal composition alters plasma competitive precursor ratios.
routes.context: Healthy-adult acute feeding experiments.
routes.limitations: Context-dependent responses, including null contrasts; no optimum or clinical benefit.

principal_route_selection.rationale: Retain Dietary Requirements as the existing admitted regulatory-state route, not a new capacity requirement. No SOP or lifestyle candidate independently establishes a preferred transport-optimisation protocol in this bounded assessment.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: No head-to-head superiority over all SOP or lifestyle routes; changes in plasma ratios are not automatically beneficial.

assessments.relevance: Regulates the measured competitive precursor presentation state.
assessments.directness: Plasma endpoint is directly measured; brain transport remains inferred.
assessments.extent: Different acute meals and proteins give different responses; no universal direction or dose target.
