connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Summarises nutritional influences discussed around the serotonergic system, including precursor and micronutrient context.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Nutrition review; it does not establish intake-responsive human brain serotonin on this mechanism.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Serotonin signalling uses receptor families, reuptake and enzymatic metabolism
scientific_findings.finding_summary: After synthesis, serotonin is released, acts on several receptor families, is taken back up by the serotonin transporter (SERT) and can be metabolised enzymatically. That sequence is signalling biology, not a dietary rule.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: This finding covers the release-and-receptor part of the Overview. It identifies later-stage dietary candidates as still unassessed. It does not admit a SERT or MAO dietary lever.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Serotonergic signalling includes vesicular handling, receptor-mediated actions, transporter-mediated reuptake and enzymatic metabolism; those stages are not interchangeable with precursor supply and are not evidence of dietary control.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The expanded-biology review describes serotonin’s receptor diversity, transporter-mediated clearance and metabolic handling as the operational signalling sequence. ADHD-focused serotonin reviews use receptor and transporter language as pharmacological and neurobiological context, not as food targets. Together they establish that signalling is more than synthesis. They do not measure diet-responsive receptor or transporter change.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Review-level coverage. Specific dietary dependencies of monoamine oxidase or of SERT function remain unassessed.

evidence_considered.label: Berger, Gray and Roth (2009)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Serotonin signalling involves multiple receptor families, transporter-mediated reuptake and further metabolic fates, including a pineal route toward melatonin.

assessment.study: Same serotonin-biology review used for PM5-F1, reused here for the signalling-sequence proposition.
assessment.population: Mixed mechanistic literature; not a dietary sample.
assessment.result: Described post-synthesis signalling stages without testing food intake.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No dietary effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Establishes release, receptor, reuptake and metabolism as part of the mechanism.
assessment.limitations: Review; no dietary or ADHD endpoint.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Faraone et al. (2025)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Systematic review of serotonin in ADHD neurobiology, including receptor and transporter context.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: ADHD literature review; not a dietary signalling measurement.

evidence_dependency: Berger, Gray and Roth (2009) is also primary evidence in PM5-F1. Reuse here answers the signalling-sequence proposition, not an independent replication of the mood-role review.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Emotional-regulation relevance is not a dietary or ADHD-treatment finding
scientific_findings.finding_summary: The attached sources support serotonin as emotion-regulation-relevant biology. They do not show that meals, tryptophan, iron or B6 change human serotonin signalling, and they do not show a uniform ADHD lesion that diet can correct.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Keep biological relevance separate from dietary modulation and from inflammation or saffron findings that are not serotonin-process measurements.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Repository and bounded-review evidence supports a translational relationship from serotonergic signalling to Emotional Regulation without establishing dietary modification of serotonin or an ADHD treatment effect.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Shaw supplies the emotion-regulation account. Faraone and Banerjee show that ADHD-related serotonin discussion is heterogeneous and cannot be restated as a single deficit. Fernstrom describes meal-level precursor transport upstream of signalling. Together they support a biology-to-emotion mapping while blocking a food-as-serotonin-treatment reading.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: No attached study measures emotional regulation after a dietary change aimed at serotonin. Plasma amino-acid ratios, inflammation connectivity and saffron trials are not serotonin signalling.

evidence_considered.label: Shaw et al. (2014)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Emotion dysregulation is a clinically important ADHD-related phenotype discussed with monoamine context, without testing diet.

assessment.study: Same emotion-dysregulation review used for PM5-F1, reused here for the Phenome-relationship proposition.
assessment.population: ADHD and comparison literature; not a dietary sample.
assessment.result: Supports emotion-regulation-relevant biology without a treatment or intake effect.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No clinical or dietary effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Anchors the Phenome mapping in signalling biology.
assessment.limitations: Review; no dietary endpoint.

evidence_considered.label: Faraone et al. (2025)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: ADHD-related serotonin findings are mixed across methods and constructs and do not support a uniform global deficit that can be treated as a serotonin-diet claim.

assessment.study: Systematic literature review of serotonin in ADHD neurobiology.
assessment.population: ADHD clinical and mechanistic literature.
assessment.result: Reported heterogeneous serotonin-related findings rather than one directional lesion.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No pooled dietary serotonin effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Constrains ADHD wording attached to this Phenome relationship.
assessment.limitations: ADHD-focused; not a serotonin dietary trial.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Fernstrom (2013)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Describes meal-level large-neutral-amino-acid transport that can change tryptophan presentation before serotonin synthesis.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Transport and plasma-ratio biology; it does not measure serotonin signalling or emotion regulation.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Jackson et al. (2021)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Saffron supplementation trial in low mood; sometimes attached to mood phenomes.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Wrong construct for this mechanism: not a serotonin-process measurement and not a Dietary Requirement.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Marsland et al. (2017)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: Links systemic inflammation to default-mode connectivity discussed near perseverative thought.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Inflammation and connectivity; it does not measure serotonin signalling.

evidence_dependency: Shaw et al. (2014) is also primary evidence in PM5-F1. Reuse here answers the Phenome-relationship proposition, not an independent replication of the signalling review.
Fernstrom (2013) is connected evidence here and primary evidence in PM5-IC1. That is one transport review used for two propositions, not two independent studies.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Precursor transport is not serotonergic signalling
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Plasma amino-acid ratios and meal-level LAT1 competition can sit next to this mechanism. They do not measure serotonin release, receptor signalling or a mood outcome of changing diet.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Use these sources to keep measurements distinct. Do not promote them as headline serotonin Findings.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: LAT1-related precursor presentation is not interchangeable with serotonergic signalling.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Fernstrom addresses competitive precursor transport, including tryptophan. That is useful as a boundary on how other evidence is read. It does not establish serotonin signalling change or a dietary mood effect.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Interpretive only. This source does not fill the missing human dietary-to-serotonin measurement.
evidence_dependency: Fernstrom (2013) is also connected evidence in PM5-F3. Reuse here constrains measurement identity, not a second transport experiment.

evidence_considered.label: Fernstrom (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Meal composition can change plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratios and therefore competitive presentation of tryptophan at LAT1.

assessment.study: Review of large-neutral-amino-acid transport and brain neurochemistry.
assessment.population: Human meal-study and mechanistic literature.
assessment.result: Showed transport-level precursor presentation, not serotonin signalling.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Plasma-ratio changes; not a serotonin-release estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Constrains transport evidence as upstream presentation.
assessment.limitations: Does not measure serotonin receptors, mood or ADHD.

decision.applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the shared indispensable-amino-acid quality pool can constrain this mechanism’s governed serotonergic capacity.
established_links: Tryptophan is indispensable and is the serotonin starting material (PM5-F2).
DIAAS and related scores measure digestible IAA adequacy for protein quality (FAO 2013; Mariotti 2019).
inferred_links: Incomplete meal protein quality would therefore lower tryptophan supply and constrain serotonin signalling.
decision.rationale: Assessment was completed. Quality-scoring evidence does not connect IAA-quality inadequacy to serotonergic capacity. Fernstrom’s protein effects operate through the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio, which is the competitive arm. Extreme tryptophan-poor diets are a different construct. The capacity-constraint link remains a material gap, not a negative finding.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Superseded scope: this proposition concerns the former broad indispensable-amino-acid quality arm. Current BRS1 KC1 is the monoamine-precursor LNAA competitive pool. Archiving does not reject general protein-quality biology or alter the separately assessed competitive/supply decisions.

decision.applicability_proposition: Imbalance of LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance can constrain this mechanism’s governed serotonergic capacity.
established_links: LAT1 competition changes tryptophan presentation (PM5-IC1; Fernstrom 2013).

established_links.Fernstrom 2013: ordinary protein-driven LNAA changes produce large variations in brain tryptophan uptake and serotonin synthesis.

inferred_links: Those synthesis-rate changes would also change serotonin release, mood or ADHD outcomes.
decision.rationale: Type D (2) is met for formation capacity: named LAT1 imbalance is connected to a constraint on serotonin synthesis, a defining capacity this mechanism governs. Transport is still not signalling (PM5-IC1). Mood, sleep and ADHD remain inference.

kc_adjudication_history.rationale: Metadata migration only: preserve the established governs/constrained-by interpretation as a typed Conditional constraint for FM summary derivation. No stronger scientific admission.

content:
## BRS1-1-5 - Serotonergic Signalling Regulation (Pathways for Mood & Behavioural Control) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Support serotonergic signalling so mood stability, inhibition, and behavioural regulation remain well grounded. **Intervention Dominance:** Diet/Lifestyle-Combined
- Tryptophan - Iron - Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP; active vitamin B6 cofactor) - Vitamin B6
- Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) Tetrahydrobiopterin is an endogenous cofactor required for tryptophan hydroxylation, not a dietary BH4 recommendation. Tryptophan as the local hydroxylase substrate is listed above. Dietary tryptophan supply is assessed on [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation). Competitive LAT1 transport is assessed on [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation).
No additional distinct KC relationship established; precursor availability is covered in §3.1.1.
### Overview Serotonin is made in neurons when tryptophan is converted through two enzyme steps, then shaped by release, receptors, reuptake and breakdown. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Across brain regions, the same transmitter can support different responses. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) That system supports mood stability, inhibition and behavioural regulation. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Tryptophan, iron and vitamin B6 are part of the chemistry. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) - **Benefits:** Serotonin signalling supports emotional regulation, impulse control and behavioural stability. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[15]](#pm-ref-15) - **Implementation Notes:** Tryptophan, iron, and vitamin B6 are the substrate and cofactor relationships. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Extra intake is not established to raise brain serotonin or improve mood or attention. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) Tetrahydrobiopterin is made in the body and is not a dietary recommendation. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) - **Biological Relevance:** This is the signalling step after tryptophan has [entered the brain](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation); circulating supply and competitive transport come first. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ serotonergic signalling capacity; ↑ emotional regulation support; ↑ stress-response modulation; ↑ behavioural inhibition; ↑ sleep-compatible neurochemical signalling ## 3. Intervention Levers

Only categories with a substantive evidence-qualified intervention are shown.

No evidence-qualified lifestyle relationship is projected.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Serotonin is a monoamine neurotransmitter synthesised from tryptophan and influenced by precursor availability, competitive amino-acid transport, micronutrient-dependent synthesis pathways, and broader metabolic context. Within [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function), serotonergic signalling operates alongside dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems to influence emotional regulation, behavioural control, stress responsiveness, and sleep-related neurobiology.
#### (Tryptophan availability and serotonin synthesis) Dietary tryptophan is the starting material for serotonin. Tryptophan hydroxylase converts it to 5-hydroxytryptophan using iron and tetrahydrobiopterin; aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase then uses PLP to form serotonin. Brain access of tryptophan also depends on competition with other large neutral amino acids at blood–brain barrier transport systems. #### (LAT1 competition and transport dynamics) Transport of tryptophan across the blood–brain barrier occurs through LAT1 transport mechanisms shared with other amino acids. Meal composition, insulin response, and amino-acid competition may influence relative brain tryptophan availability → [Fernstrom, 2013] #### (Serotonergic regulation and emotional function) Serotonin participates in emotional processing, behavioural inhibition, stress regulation, and impulse control. Alterations in serotonergic signalling have been associated with emotional dysregulation and impulsive behavioural phenotypes → [Shaw et al., 2014] [Banerjee and Nandagopal, 2015] #### (Monoaminergic integration) Serotonergic signalling does not operate independently. Functional outcomes emerge through interaction with dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems as part of broader monoaminergic regulation represented under [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function). #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Amino-acid pool sufficiency belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation). LNAA competitive transport belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). Noradrenergic attention context belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM4](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation).
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Enzyme studies and biochemical reviews establish the neuronal tryptophan-to-serotonin synthesis sequence and its cofactor dependence. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Broader reviews support receptor diversity and transporter-mediated handling as additional determinants of serotonergic function. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Together, the evidence supports synthesis and signalling as related but distinct capacities; it does not directly establish that ordinary dietary changes regulate human brain serotonin or produce uniform functional benefits. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM3 — Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) ↓ [BRS1-FM1-PM5 — Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) — Pineal conversion of serotonin toward melatonin can use SAM from one-carbon metabolism. The attached corpus does not establish that ordinary methylation-cycle variation controls serotonergic signalling, mood or sleep. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) — Supplies the circulating amino-acid pool, including tryptophan used to make serotonin. Amino-acid quality and precursor-pool adequacy are assessed there. That is precursor supply, not serotonin signalling. - [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — Governs competitive brain entry of large neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, after a meal. Transport bias is not serotonin synthesis or receptor signalling. - [BRS1-FM1-PM3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — Parallel catecholamine path that shares LAT1 presentation and some decarboxylase chemistry. Dopaminergic signalling is not serotonergic signalling. - [BRS1-FM1-PM4 - Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — Parallel monoamine path from shared precursor transport. It does not form serotonin. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Each Phenome relationship has two independent ratings. They are not combined or averaged.

Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength

How direct and important is this biological mechanism expected to be to the Phenome within the BRAIN model?

Evidence Confidence

How strongly does the adjudicated evidence support this particular biology → Phenome relationship?

Emotional Regulation — supports Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** High - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Serotonin signalling is a core biological substrate for emotional regulation, impulse control and affective stability Shaw et al. (2014) [[4]](#pm-ref-4). ADHD-focused serotonin reviews do not establish a uniform serotonin deficit that diet can correct Faraone et al. 2025 [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Banerjee and Nandagopal (2015) [[5]](#pm-ref-5). **Supporting evidence**
Stress Resilience — supports Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low–Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Serotonin signalling participates in emotional processing and stress-related control Shaw et al. (2014) [[4]](#pm-ref-4). The attached sources do not measure stress resilience after a dietary change aimed at serotonin Tang et al. 2025 [[2]](#pm-ref-2).
Sleep / Calming Tone — supports Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low - **Rationale:** Serotonin participates in sleep–wake and calming neurochemistry Berger, Gray and Roth (2009) [[15]](#pm-ref-15). Meal-level precursor transport is not a sleep outcome Fernstrom (2013) [[1]](#pm-ref-1).
Reward Regulation — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low - **Evidence Confidence:** Low - **Rationale:** Serotonin can interact with dopaminergic reward circuits and behavioural inhibition Faraone et al. 2025 [[3]](#pm-ref-3). That interaction is not a measured reward outcome after diet Tang et al. 2025 [[2]](#pm-ref-2).
Apprehensive Worry / Perseverative Thought — supports Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low–Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Serotonin signalling intersects negative-valence and control circuits discussed in mood and anxiety contexts Briguglio et al. (2018) [[6]](#pm-ref-6). Systemic-inflammation connectivity is not a serotonin measurement Marsland et al. (2017) [[7]](#pm-ref-7).
Pleasure & Interest Capacity — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low–Medium - **Evidence Confidence:** Low–Medium - **Rationale:** Serotonin pathways sit near positive-valence mood biology Berger, Gray and Roth (2009) [[15]](#pm-ref-15). Saffron supplementation trials are not serotonin-process measurements and are not a Dietary Requirement of this mechanism Jackson et al. (2021) [[8]](#pm-ref-8).
Social Engagement Capacity — modulates Open Page → →
- **Biology → Phenome Relationship Strength:** Low - **Evidence Confidence:** Low - **Rationale:** Serotonin can modulate affiliative and social-affective behaviour in translational accounts Berger, Gray and Roth (2009) [[15]](#pm-ref-15). A saffron social-relationship outcome is not a serotonin signalling measurement Jackson et al. (2021) [[8]](#pm-ref-8).

title: Synaptic Structural Plasticity
mission: Maintain and adapt physical connections between neurons through synapse formation, selective stabilisation, structural remodelling and elimination.
rationale: Recent bounded assessment preserves synaptic structure versus membrane incorporation. Combined choline/uridine/DHA exposures, age/model and human delivery need exact attribution before food-specific structural claims.

data.title: Synaptic Structural Plasticity
data.mission: Maintain and adapt physical connections between neurons through synapse formation, selective stabilisation, structural remodelling and elimination.
data.summary: Neural circuits adapt partly by changing their physical connections. New connections can form, useful ones can persist, and others can be resized or removed. This supports a biological basis for learning and adaptation; increasing connection counts alone is not the goal. The clearest direct structural evidence reviewed here is from animals and neuronal slices, rather than human synapse measurements.
data.dose_sensitivity: Learning, sleep, activity and experimental feeding effects depend on the studied species, region, exposure and age; no human synapse-growth dose is established.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Learning forms and selectively stabilises dendritic spines
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Motor learning in mice produces new dendritic spines and selectively retains a subset as other spines are eliminated.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Motor learning in mice produces new dendritic spines and selectively retains a subset as other spines are eliminated.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Adaptation concerns which connections persist, not simply increasing their number.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Longitudinal imaging links learned tasks with spine formation and persistence. Spine measurements are retained as such; behavioural association does not prove that every observed spine is a new functional synapse.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mouse motor cortex and task-specific learning; no human training dose or general cognitive benefit inferred.

evidence_considered.label: Xu et al. (2009)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: New spines appeared rapidly and training selectively stabilised some, alongside elimination of pre-existing spines.

assessment.study: Longitudinal in-vivo two-photon imaging during forelimb motor learning.
assessment.population: Mice; motor cortex.
assessment.result: New spines appeared rapidly and training selectively stabilised some, alongside elimination of pre-existing spines.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Formation detectable within one hour; no universal density target.
assessment.evidence_summary: New spines appeared rapidly and training selectively stabilised some, alongside elimination of pre-existing spines.
assessment.limitations: Morphological spine observations and motor performance are separate endpoints; each spine was not independently verified ultrastructurally.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary source abstract and indexed Results/Methods examined.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Local signalling and cytoskeletal remodelling stabilise spine changes
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Activity can induce local BDNF–TrkB signalling and staged actin and postsynaptic scaffold remodelling at individual dendritic spines.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Activity can induce local BDNF–TrkB signalling and staged actin and postsynaptic scaffold remodelling at individual dendritic spines.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Structural change and altered synaptic transmission can accompany one another without being interchangeable measurements.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Single-spine experiments identify local signalling and cytoskeletal reorganisation rather than a new dietary cofactor list.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Hippocampal slice experiments; artificial stimulation and molecular interventions do not establish ordinary dietary responsiveness.

evidence_considered.label: Bosch et al. (2014)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Actin/cofilin reorganised early; scaffold remodelling followed in a later protein-synthesis-dependent phase.

assessment.study: Glutamate uncaging with fluorescent protein and volume imaging during structural LTP.
assessment.population: Rat hippocampal slice cultures.
assessment.result: Actin/cofilin reorganised early; scaffold remodelling followed in a later protein-synthesis-dependent phase.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Distinct temporal phases; not a count of newly formed synapses.
assessment.evidence_summary: Actin/cofilin reorganised early; scaffold remodelling followed in a later protein-synthesis-dependent phase.
assessment.limitations: Structural LTP is the readout; protein abundance and spine volume are not cognition.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full author-hosted primary PDF: Results, Figures 1–7 and Methods.

evidence_considered.label: Harward et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Postsynaptic BDNF release and local TrkB activation contributed to structural potentiation.

assessment.study: Single-spine TrkB sensor imaging and BDNF pathway manipulation.
assessment.population: Cultured rodent hippocampal slices.
assessment.result: Postsynaptic BDNF release and local TrkB activation contributed to structural potentiation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Local spine signalling; no population-wide intervention estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Postsynaptic BDNF release and local TrkB activation contributed to structural potentiation.
assessment.limitations: Slice stimulation is not food exposure; no dietary BDNF requirement follows.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary source abstract and indexed Results/Methods examined.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Sleep supports selective formation, pruning and resizing
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Mouse studies associate sleep with task-related spine formation, REM-dependent selective pruning and reduced size of many ultrastructurally identified synaptic contacts.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Mouse studies associate sleep with task-related spine formation, REM-dependent selective pruning and reduced size of many ultrastructurally identified synaptic contacts.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Formation, elimination and resizing are complementary processes; sleep is not uniformly synapse-increasing.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Different experiments resolve post-learning formation, REM-dependent selection and wake/sleep scaling. Their regions, ages and endpoints differ.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Preclinical contexts; no universal sleep duration, clinical programme or human synapse effect is established.

evidence_considered.label: Yang et al. (2014)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Post-learning sleep promoted formation of new spines on selected dendritic branches.

assessment.study: Motor learning followed by sleep or sleep deprivation with longitudinal imaging.
assessment.population: Mice; motor cortex.
assessment.result: Post-learning sleep promoted formation of new spines on selected dendritic branches.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Branch-specific morphological response, not whole-brain synapse number.
assessment.evidence_summary: Post-learning sleep promoted formation of new spines on selected dendritic branches.
assessment.limitations: Learning and sleep exposure interact; reactivation and formation are not proof of a general human benefit.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full primary author manuscript/PDF and indexed Results.

evidence_considered.label: Li et al. (2017)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: REM sleep pruned some new spines while strengthening and maintaining others.

assessment.study: REM manipulations and repeated spine imaging during development and motor learning.
assessment.population: Developing and motor-trained mice.
assessment.result: REM sleep pruned some new spines while strengthening and maintaining others.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Selective elimination and maintenance; no single beneficial direction.
assessment.evidence_summary: REM sleep pruned some new spines while strengthening and maintaining others.
assessment.limitations: Developmental and learning contexts must remain distinct; no adult-human pruning prescription.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary source abstract and indexed Results/Methods examined.

evidence_considered.label: de Vivo et al. (2017)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Axon–spine interfaces were smaller after sleep, with large synapses relatively spared.

assessment.study: Serial three-dimensional electron microscopy after sleep or wake.
assessment.population: Mouse motor and sensory cortices; 6,920 sampled synapses.
assessment.result: Axon–spine interfaces were smaller after sleep, with large synapses relatively spared.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Approximately 18% smaller interfaces; synapses are nested within animals, not 6,920 independent subjects.
assessment.evidence_summary: Axon–spine interfaces were smaller after sleep, with large synapses relatively spared.
assessment.limitations: Cross-sectional ultrastructure, not longitudinal tracking or proof that every reduction improves memory.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract and author-manuscript Results/table methods examined.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Inhibitory contacts also undergo experience-related structural remodelling
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In adult mouse neocortex, inhibitory synapse markers and dendritic spines show spatially related structural dynamics influenced by sensory experience.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In adult mouse neocortex, inhibitory synapse markers and dendritic spines show spatially related structural dynamics influenced by sensory experience.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Structural plasticity includes inhibitory contacts, rather than only excitatory spine density.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Inhibitory postsynaptic gephyrin imaging complements excitatory spine observations and ultrastructural validation in the original study.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: A marker-based longitudinal signal is not automatically a census of all inhibitory functional synapses or an E/I-balance measurement.

evidence_considered.label: Chen et al. (2012)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Inhibitory-contact changes clustered near changing spines and responded to sensory input.

assessment.study: Longitudinal in-vivo inhibitory gephyrin and spine imaging with altered visual experience.
assessment.population: Adult mouse neocortex.
assessment.result: Inhibitory-contact changes clustered near changing spines and responded to sensory input.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Spatial clustering; no generic increase in inhibitory synapse number claimed.
assessment.evidence_summary: Inhibitory-contact changes clustered near changing spines and responded to sensory input.
assessment.limitations: Selected dendrites and marker-defined contacts; not all inhibitory circuit types.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Indexed full primary Results/Figures 3–5 and publisher record; direct PDF access failed.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Developmental microglia participate in selective synaptic elimination
scientific_findings.finding_summary: In the developing mouse visual pathway, microglia engulf presynaptic inputs through activity-sensitive complement signalling.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: In the developing mouse visual pathway, microglia engulf presynaptic inputs through activity-sensitive complement signalling.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Selective removal is part of circuit organisation; indiscriminate elimination is not a health target.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Activity and CR3/C3 manipulations establish a pruning process in a defined postnatal circuit.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Developmental visual circuitry is not evidence for a human diet-driven or adult injury-repair intervention.

evidence_considered.label: Schafer et al. (2012)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Disrupting CR3/C3 signalling altered engulfment and left persistent connectivity deficits.

assessment.study: Activity manipulation and CR3/C3 disruption with engulfment/connectivity analyses.
assessment.population: Postnatal mouse retinogeniculate pathway.
assessment.result: Disrupting CR3/C3 signalling altered engulfment and left persistent connectivity deficits.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Genetic/activity-dependent effects; no intake or clinical effect size.
assessment.evidence_summary: Disrupting CR3/C3 signalling altered engulfment and left persistent connectivity deficits.
assessment.limitations: Developmental context and circuit specificity; does not justify boosting complement or generic inflammation.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full author-hosted primary PDF, Results and Figures 1–7.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Membrane precursors and a tested combination have different evidence roles
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Uridine and choline contribute to membrane-precursor supply; DHA with UMP increased hippocampal spine density in adult gerbils, while UMP alone did not significantly increase that endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Uridine and choline contribute to membrane-precursor supply; DHA with UMP increased hippocampal spine density in adult gerbils, while UMP alone did not significantly increase that endpoint.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: A precursor role, a combination structural effect and functional benefit require separate conclusions.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Brain-slice and gerbil precursor measurements support the Kennedy supply route. In the structural experiment, choline was present in all diets; it was not isolated as an intervention. The link from phospholipid provision to structural assembly is a supported material-supply interpretation, not measured mediation.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Spines and synaptic proteins are not verified synapse counts. Endogenous synthesis also supplies precursors; animal supplementation does not establish a food dose or human benefit.

evidence_considered.label: Sakamoto et al. (2007)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: DHA alone increased spine density; co-supplementation with UMP increased it further; UMP alone was not significant for spine density.

assessment.study: Four-week DHA/UMP factorial feeding and hippocampal DiI spine imaging, phospholipid and protein assays.
assessment.population: Adult male gerbils; diet contained 0.1% choline.
assessment.result: DHA alone increased spine density; co-supplementation with UMP increased it further; UMP alone was not significant for spine density.
assessment.effect_magnitude: DHA alone +19%; DHA plus UMP +36% versus control; Fig. 2. Small animal-level imaging sample.
assessment.evidence_summary: DHA alone increased spine density; co-supplementation with UMP increased it further; UMP alone was not significant for spine density.
assessment.limitations: Counts of neurons/spines are not independent animals. No isolated choline effect or confirmed new functional synapse count.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary indexed Results §2.2, Methods §4.1–4.3 and Figures 1–4; direct PMC access blocked.

evidence_considered.label: Ulus et al. (2006)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Uridine increased utilisation of choline for CDP-choline formation.

assessment.study: Uridine/cytidine and choline exposures with CDP-choline analysis.
assessment.population: Rat brain slices.
assessment.result: Uridine increased utilisation of choline for CDP-choline formation.
assessment.effect_magnitude: 61% at 400 micromolar uridine in the assessed experiment.
assessment.evidence_summary: Uridine increased utilisation of choline for CDP-choline formation.
assessment.limitations: Kennedy intermediate, not a spine measurement, oral dose or synapse-mediated benefit.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Reuse of verified PM7-F8 primary full-text assessment.

evidence_considered.label: Cansev et al. (2005)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: UMP increased brain uridine and nucleotide/CDP-choline pools transiently.

assessment.study: Single oral UMP with serial brain precursor assays.
assessment.population: Adult gerbils.
assessment.result: UMP increased brain uridine and nucleotide/CDP-choline pools transiently.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Precursor concentrations increased; not an absolute membrane-synthesis flux.
assessment.evidence_summary: UMP increased brain uridine and nucleotide/CDP-choline pools transiently.
assessment.limitations: UMP is the tested phosphorylated preparation, not interchangeable with ordinary dietary uridine.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Reuse of verified PM7-F8 publisher Results/abstract.

evidence_considered.label: Wurtman et al. (2006)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Brain phospholipid abundance and synaptic proteins increased with the tested precursor exposures.

assessment.study: Four-week UMP/DHA supplementation with choline-containing chow.
assessment.population: Adult gerbils.
assessment.result: Brain phospholipid abundance and synaptic proteins increased with the tested precursor exposures.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Biochemical abundance/protein endpoints, not a direct synapse census.
assessment.evidence_summary: Brain phospholipid abundance and synaptic proteins increased with the tested precursor exposures.
assessment.limitations: Combination and endogenous supply; no isolated choline efficacy or cognitive mediation.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Reuse of verified PM7-F8 primary full-text assessment.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Voluntary running changes spine and dendritic structure in rats
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Two months of voluntary running changed dendritic spine density and selected dendritic structures in adult rat hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Two months of voluntary running changed dendritic spine density and selected dendritic structures in adult rat hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Physical activity can influence structure in this model; structural changes do not by themselves establish human cognitive benefit.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Golgi and DiI measurements extend evidence beyond dentate neurogenesis to existing neuronal dendrites.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Rat voluntary running and selected regions; no human exercise dose, synapse count or mediation claim.

evidence_considered.label: Stranahan et al. (2007)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Running increased spine density in selected hippocampal and entorhinal neurons, with region-dependent morphological changes.

assessment.study: Two-month voluntary wheel access versus sedentary housing; Golgi and DiI morphology.
assessment.population: Adult rats.
assessment.result: Running increased spine density in selected hippocampal and entorhinal neurons, with region-dependent morphological changes.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Regional morphological differences; no translated human effect estimate.
assessment.evidence_summary: Running increased spine density in selected hippocampal and entorhinal neurons, with region-dependent morphological changes.
assessment.limitations: Not a universal effect across all neurons; structure and cognitive outcomes were not jointly proven causal.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full author-hosted primary PDF, Results and Methods.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Ageing-related presynaptic enlargement is a separate structural endpoint
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic active zones and excess vesicle release in fruit flies without rescuing the age-related loss of synapse number.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic active zones and excess vesicle release in fruit flies without rescuing the age-related loss of synapse number.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Preserving organisation can differ from increasing counts; a fly intervention is not a human requirement or established memory treatment.
scientific_findings.synthesis: The study combines molecular, ultrastructural and release measurements with behavioural/genetic analyses. Its structural proposition is narrower than general synaptogenesis.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Invertebrate ageing model. The human wheat-germ-extract trial did not improve its primary memory endpoint and did not directly measure synaptic structure.

evidence_considered.label: Gupta et al. (2016)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Feeding prevented active-zone enlargement and increased release accompanying ageing; reduced synapse counts were not restored.

assessment.study: Spermidine feeding with active-zone imaging/EM, release reporters and genetic analyses.
assessment.population: Young and aged Drosophila.
assessment.result: Feeding prevented active-zone enlargement and increased release accompanying ageing; reduced synapse counts were not restored.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Endpoint-specific prevention, not whole-brain synapse growth.
assessment.evidence_summary: Feeding prevented active-zone enlargement and increased release accompanying ageing; reduced synapse counts were not restored.
assessment.limitations: Fly ageing; cannot infer benefit from human supplementation or ordinary foods.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full primary PLOS Results, active-zone/EM analyses and synapse-number section.

connected_supportive_evidence.label: Schwarz et al. (2022)
connected_supportive_evidence.why_relevant: A 12-month randomised wheat-germ-extract trial in 100 older adults with subjective cognitive decline did not improve the primary memory endpoint.
connected_supportive_evidence.why_excluded: Human memory outcome without direct synaptic structural measurement; not the same preparation or biological context as fly spermidine feeding.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Glucocorticoid exposure regulates spine turnover in context
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Mouse experiments show glucocorticoid-dependent spine formation and elimination, with different effects of physiological and prolonged exposures.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Mouse experiments show glucocorticoid-dependent spine formation and elimination, with different effects of physiological and prolonged exposures.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Hormonal exposure is a structural context, not proof that a named stress-management practice changes spines.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Longitudinal imaging separates formation from elimination during developmental and adult exposure conditions.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mouse dose/timing contexts; no generic cortisol-lowering, stress protocol or injury-repair benefit inferred.

evidence_considered.label: Liston and Gan (2011)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Exposure context altered spine turnover; prolonged exposure promoted loss of established spines.

assessment.study: In-vivo spine imaging with glucocorticoid exposure and pathway manipulation.
assessment.population: Developing and adult mice.
assessment.result: Exposure context altered spine turnover; prolonged exposure promoted loss of established spines.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Direction depended on exposure duration and context.
assessment.evidence_summary: Exposure context altered spine turnover; prolonged exposure promoted loss of established spines.
assessment.limitations: Manipulating glucocorticoids does not isolate the effects of mindfulness, autonomic practices or ordinary stress reduction.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary source abstract and indexed Results/Methods examined.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Developmental DHA responses include synaptic markers and cortical function
scientific_findings.finding_summary: DHA exposure from birth increased pre- and postsynaptic marker abundance in mouse visual cortex; cultured neurons showed additional contact-marker and network responses.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: DHA exposure from birth increased pre- and postsynaptic marker abundance in mouse visual cortex; cultured neurons showed additional contact-marker and network responses.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: Developmental synaptic markers, in-vitro contacts and visually evoked responses remain separate endpoints, rather than a verified whole-brain synapse census.
scientific_findings.synthesis: DHA exposure from birth increased pre- and postsynaptic marker abundance in mouse visual cortex; cultured neurons showed additional contact-marker and network responses.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: DHA supplementation from birth and cultured-neuron exposure; not an adult-human effect or ordinary-food target.

evidence_considered.label: Carbone et al. (2020)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: DHA increased synaptic-marker abundance and promoted visual-response maturation; in vitro contact markers and network activity changed.

assessment.study: Daily oral DHA from postnatal day 1, cortical marker quantification and visually evoked recordings; complementary neuronal cultures.
assessment.population: Developing mice and cultured rodent neurons.
assessment.result: DHA increased synaptic-marker abundance and promoted visual-response maturation; in vitro contact markers and network activity changed.
assessment.effect_magnitude: 300 mg/kg/day in pups; visual and structural endpoints assessed separately.
assessment.evidence_summary: DHA increased synaptic-marker abundance and promoted visual-response maturation; in vitro contact markers and network activity changed.
assessment.limitations: Marker puncta do not independently verify every contact. Culture, development and adult gerbil findings must not be pooled as one endpoint.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Full publisher Methods, Results and Figures; online publication 2019, journal issue 2020.

scientific_findings.finding_label: Meal scheduling changes regional spine maintenance under obesogenic exposure
scientific_findings.finding_summary: Active-period feeding altered regional spine maintenance in mice previously exposed to high-fat/high-sucrose feeding, alongside memory and activity responses.
scientific_findings.finding_statement: Active-period feeding altered regional spine maintenance in mice previously exposed to high-fat/high-sucrose feeding, alongside memory and activity responses.
scientific_findings.finding_interpretation: An intervention can change structural dynamics in opposite regional directions; benefit is not equivalent to maximising spine retention.
scientific_findings.synthesis: Active-period feeding altered regional spine maintenance in mice previously exposed to high-fat/high-sucrose feeding, alongside memory and activity responses.
scientific_findings.synthesis_limitations: Mouse obesogenic exposure and four-week feeding schedule. Structural and behavioural measurements do not establish a general human fasting benefit.

evidence_considered.label: Chakraborty et al. (2025)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Feeding schedules corrected regionally opposed maintenance changes accompanying obesogenic exposure.

assessment.study: Diet exposure since weaning, then four weeks of active-period time-restricted feeding with longitudinal spine imaging.
assessment.population: Male and female mice; structural groups of six animals.
assessment.result: Feeding schedules corrected regionally opposed maintenance changes accompanying obesogenic exposure.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Food access zt11–zt1; region- and endpoint-specific changes, not a universal increase in counts.
assessment.evidence_summary: Feeding schedules corrected regionally opposed maintenance changes accompanying obesogenic exposure.
assessment.limitations: No human eating window, nutrient-specific attribution or ordinary healthy-adult benefit. Food was the same within diet groups.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Indexed primary Methods and spine formation/elimination/maintenance figures; direct publisher/PMC opening blocked.

data.scientific_findings_intro: Longitudinal animal imaging supports task-related spine formation and selective retention; sleep experiments add pruning and resizing, including electron-microscopy-confirmed contacts. Local signalling, actin remodelling and developmental microglial engulfment explain distinct steps. Nutrient experiments show membrane-precursor responses and a DHA–UMP spine effect, not verified human synapse growth. Excitatory spine, inhibitory-marker, ultrastructural, protein and behavioural endpoints remain separate. A developmental DHA study adds contact-marker and cortical-function evidence; defined meal scheduling changes regional maintenance under obesogenic exposure. These contexts do not establish ordinary adult-human benefits.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Choline supplies the phosphocholine headgroup used to build phosphatidylcholine, a membrane material supporting structural assembly.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: This is membrane-precursor provision through the Kennedy route. Choline was not isolated in the gerbil spine experiment; no increased human synapse number or benefit from extra intake is established.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: Uridine can supply CTP used in CDP-choline and phosphatidylcholine formation, contributing membrane precursors for structural assembly.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: Endogenous nucleotide synthesis and salvage also contribute. UMP alone did not significantly increase gerbil spine density; that null structural result does not erase the precursor role. No ordinary-food dose or human structural benefit is established.

dietary_input_traceability.dietary_input_note: Accepted dietary provision or constituent supply relationship; no efficacy or quantity claim added.
dietary_input_traceability.biological_role: DHA supplementation increased hippocampal dendritic spine density in adult gerbils in the studied four-week exposure.
dietary_input_traceability.evidence_limitation: This is a preclinical structural state response, not proof of an indispensable intake or verified new synapse counts. It does not establish human synapse growth, ordinary-food equivalence or cognitive benefit. Developmental mouse marker and visual-response evidence is additional, context-specific support; marker abundance is not an ultrastructurally verified contact count.

dietary_lever_presentations.label: Choline
dietary_lever_presentations.reader_description: Choline supplies the phosphocholine headgroup used to build phosphatidylcholine, a membrane material supporting structural assembly.

dietary_lever_presentations.label: Uridine
dietary_lever_presentations.reader_description: Uridine can supply CTP used in CDP-choline and phosphatidylcholine formation, contributing membrane precursors for structural assembly.

dietary_lever_presentations.label: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
dietary_lever_presentations.reader_description: DHA supplementation increased hippocampal dendritic spine density in adult gerbils in the studied four-week exposure.

system_optimisation_practices.biological_role: DHA plus uridine monophosphate (UMP) increased gerbil hippocampal spine density more than DHA alone in the tested exposure.
system_optimisation_practices.evidence_limitation: Four weeks, choline present in all diets, small animal-level sample. UMP alone was not significant for spine density. This is an experimental combination, not a human supplementation recommendation.
system_optimisation_practices.reader_description: DHA plus uridine monophosphate (UMP) increased gerbil hippocampal spine density more than DHA alone in the tested exposure.

system_optimisation_practices.biological_role: Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic release sites in fruit flies.
system_optimisation_practices.evidence_limitation: It did not restore reduced synapse numbers. Human wheat-germ-extract memory results were null; neither those results nor the fly study establish human structural benefit.
system_optimisation_practices.reader_description: Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic release sites in fruit flies.

canonical_identity.reason: Substance page exists, but canonical registry membership was not found.

system_optimisation_practices.biological_role: A defined active-period feeding schedule changed regional spine maintenance in mice exposed to an obesogenic diet.
system_optimisation_practices.evidence_limitation: Four-week mouse protocol after prolonged high-fat/high-sucrose exposure. Regionally opposite structural responses; no human eating-window target or general healthy-adult benefit established.
system_optimisation_practices.reader_description: Meal scheduling changed the maintenance of connections differently across brain regions in this mouse diet model.

lifestyle_priorities.biological_role: Learning and practising a new motor skill can form and selectively stabilise dendritic spines in mice.
lifestyle_priorities.evidence_limitation: Mouse motor tasks and spine imaging; not a human practice dose, verified synapse count or general cognitive-treatment claim.
lifestyle_priorities.reader_description: Learning and practising a new motor skill can form and selectively stabilise dendritic spines in mice.

lifestyle_priorities.biological_role: Sleep can support formation, selective retention, removal and resizing of connections after learning.
lifestyle_priorities.evidence_limitation: Mouse sleep/REM manipulations and ultrastructure differ by age, region and endpoint. More spines is not always better; no universal human sleep duration is derived.
lifestyle_priorities.reader_description: Sleep can support formation, selective retention, removal and resizing of connections after learning.

lifestyle_priorities.biological_role: Voluntary running changed spine density and dendritic structure in selected regions of adult rat brains.
lifestyle_priorities.evidence_limitation: Two-month rat wheel-running exposure; no human exercise prescription, synapse-mediated cognitive effect or uniform whole-brain change is established.
lifestyle_priorities.reader_description: Voluntary running changed spine density and dendritic structure in selected regions of adult rat brains.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: The canonical monoamine precursor competitive pool supplies or constrains synaptic structural adaptation beyond its transmitter-specific role.
established_links: The canonical KC defines monoamine precursor/LNAA competitive supply, not a general structural protein pool.
Neural activity can trigger local structural remodelling (PM12-F2).
inferred_links: A general activity connection does not establish this specific pool-to-structural-process relationship.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: No canonical constituent is automatically imported. A specific source-supported supply or limiting chain for this pool remains unestablished; lack of a human end-to-end trial is not the exclusion reason.
kc_applicability_adjudications.remaining_gap: Evidence connecting the canonical competitive precursor pool to a defined structural job rather than generic transmitter participation.

kc_applicability_adjudications.applicability_proposition: The canonical methyl-donor pool has a separately supported upstream supply or conditional constraint relationship to synaptic structural adaptation.
established_links: Choline and uridine have independently assessed Kennedy membrane-precursor roles (PM12-F6).
Choline membership of KC1 is separate from PM-specific pool applicability.
inferred_links: A methylation-supported membrane route might contribute structural material, but the current structural corpus does not establish a distinct pool job beyond the published provision relationships.
kc_applicability_adjudications.rationale: Do not infer a PM12 pool constraint from choline membership, a PC relationship or homocysteine effects. No automatic admission or scientific assertion of non-existence.
kc_applicability_adjudications.remaining_gap: A supported context-specific pool-to-membrane-to-structural-process chain and distinctness adjudication beyond already admitted provision.

stage2ab_assessment_history.reason: New canonical structural-plasticity mechanism; accepted FM5 parent and mission with selective elimination.
stage2ab_assessment_history.scope: Formation, stabilisation, remodelling and elimination; separate development, healthy adaptation, ageing and injury.

pending_actions.required_action: Reconcile the existing page with canonical registry identity before any substance-based relationship projection.
pending_actions.subsequent_food_assessment: Food occurrence does not establish equivalence with experimental fly supplementation.

evidence_qualification.label: Lifestyle-Dominant
evidence_qualification.rationale: Learning, sleep and activity directly change structural endpoints across distinct animal experiments; nutritional structural modulation is narrower and precursor supply alone is not intervention efficacy.
evidence_qualification.scope_note: Principal lifestyle relevance is supported preclinically; no comparative human efficacy ranking or general synapse-increasing target is established.

routes.intervention_effect: Learning and sleep influence formation, selective retention, pruning and resizing; running changes regional morphology.
routes.context: Mouse learning/sleep and adult rat running experiments.
routes.limitations: Species, ages and endpoints differ; no human synapse-growth dose or clinical benefit.

routes.intervention_effect: DHA alone increased hippocampal spine density in the tested gerbil experiment.
routes.context: Adult male gerbils, four-week oral supplementation. Developmental mouse supplementation provides additional marker/function evidence, separately interpreted.
routes.limitations: Spine density, not verified synapse counts or human benefit.

routes.intervention_effect: DHA–UMP combination changed gerbil spine density; spermidine altered ageing-related fly active-zone structure. Active-period meal scheduling altered regional maintenance under obesogenic exposure.
routes.context: Distinct experimental supplementation preparations and species. Defined active-period feeding in mice with obesogenic exposure.
routes.limitations: No human structural benefit or clinical supplementation protocol established.

principal_route_selection.rationale: The assessed lifestyle group directly spans multiple defining structural jobs, including selective formation, persistence and elimination. Dietary structural responses cover narrower experimental endpoints, while precursor supply does not establish efficacy. Lifestyle is the principal mechanism-specific teaching route in this preclinical evidence set.
principal_route_selection.comparative_limitations: This is not a head-to-head human efficacy ranking; regional spine changes, synapse ultrastructure and benefit remain distinct. The selection does not prescribe maximising counts.

assessments.relevance: Directly covers learning-related formation/stabilisation, sleep selection and activity-associated remodelling.
assessments.directness: Longitudinal spine imaging and independently measured synaptic ultrastructure in animals.
assessments.extent: Several mission-defining structural steps and contexts; human translation remains unresolved.

content:
## BRS1-5-12 - Synaptic Structural Plasticity (Formation, selective retention, remodelling and elimination) ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Maintain and adapt physical connections between neurons through synapse formation, selective stabilisation, structural remodelling and elimination. ### Overview Neural circuits adapt partly by changing their physical connections. New connections can form, useful ones can persist, and others can be resized or removed. This supports a biological basis for learning and adaptation; increasing connection counts alone is not the goal. The clearest direct structural evidence reviewed here is from animals and neuronal slices, rather than human synapse measurements. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Li et al. (2017) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) - **Benefits:** Selective structural adaptation provides a biological basis for retaining learned skills and adapting circuits. The animal studies do not establish a human cognitive treatment. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Li et al. (2017) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) - **Implementation Notes:** Skill practice, sleep and physical activity are the most directly relevant assessed behaviours. Nutrient supply and experimental combinations have separate, bounded evidence; the studies do not provide a human synapse-growth prescription. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Yang et al. (2014) [[4]](#pm-ref-4); Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9); Stranahan et al. (2007) [[13]](#pm-ref-13) - **Biological Relevance:** Physical circuit organisation supports neuronal communication alongside transmitter signalling. Membrane production and DHA incorporation provide supporting material processes, while developmental pruning and ageing require their own context. Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Chen et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8); Gupta et al. (2016) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) ## 2. Primary Biological Effects Formation and persistence of selected dendritic spines; actin and scaffold remodelling; inhibitory-contact dynamics; developmental pruning; sleep-associated synaptic resizing. These are different structural endpoints, not a single measure of better cognition. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); de Vivo et al. (2017) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Chen et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) ## 3. Intervention Levers
- Choline - Uridine - Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
No evidence-supported cofactors or substrates are currently established for this mechanism.
No mapping established.
Experimental structural exposures are distinct from human supplementation recommendations. Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9); Gupta et al. (2016) [[14]](#pm-ref-14)
DHA plus uridine monophosphate (UMP) increased gerbil hippocampal spine density more than DHA alone in the tested exposure. **Expanded Disclosure** **Input** = Experimental DHA–UMP co-supplementation **Input type** = defined dietary exposure **Biological role** = DHA plus uridine monophosphate (UMP) increased gerbil hippocampal spine density more than DHA alone in the tested exposure. **Evidence source** = Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) **Limitation** = Four weeks, choline present in all diets, small animal-level sample. UMP alone was not significant for spine density. This is an experimental combination, not a human supplementation recommendation. Supporting mechanism research: [Membrane precursors and a tested combination have different evidence roles](#pm12-f6)
Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic release sites in fruit flies. **Expanded Disclosure** **Input** = Experimental spermidine supplementation in ageing **Input type** = defined dietary exposure **Biological role** = Spermidine feeding prevented ageing-related enlargement of presynaptic release sites in fruit flies. **Evidence source** = Gupta et al. (2016) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) **Limitation** = It did not restore reduced synapse numbers. Human wheat-germ-extract memory results were null; neither those results nor the fly study establish human structural benefit. Supporting mechanism research: [Ageing-related presynaptic enlargement is a separate structural endpoint](#pm12-f8)

(2025) [[18]](#pm-ref-18) **Limitation** = Four-week mouse protocol after prolonged high-fat/high-sucrose exposure. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) **Limitation** = Mouse motor tasks and spine imaging; not a human practice dose, verified synapse count or general cognitive-treatment claim. (2007) [[13]](#pm-ref-13) **Limitation** = Two-month rat wheel-running exposure; no human exercise prescription, synapse-mediated cognitive effect or uniform whole-brain change is established. Supporting mechanism research: [Voluntary running changes spine and dendritic structure in rats](#pm12-f7)
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Structural adaptation combines local activity-dependent remodelling with the formation, persistence and elimination of contacts. Synapse number, contact size, spine shape and transmission strength must be distinguished. Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); de Vivo et al. (2017) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)
#### (Formation and selective stabilisation) Experience can recruit new dendritic spines, while later selection retains some and removes others. Local actin and postsynaptic proteins reorganise on different timescales; BDNF–TrkB signalling can participate at an individual spine. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Harward et al. (2016) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) #### (Remodelling and elimination) Sleep studies show both formation and selective removal, as well as resizing of ultrastructurally identified contacts. Developing microglia can engulf presynaptic inputs through activity-sensitive complement signalling; this is a developmental circuit finding, not an instruction to increase pruning. Yang et al. (2014) [[4]](#pm-ref-4); Li et al. (2017) [[5]](#pm-ref-5); de Vivo et al. (2017) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) #### (Material supply and structural modulation) The Kennedy pathway supplies phosphatidylcholine membrane material. Uridine supports nucleotide provision and choline supplies a headgroup precursor. Gerbil DHA–UMP feeding produced a spine-density response, but the experiment does not prove that increased membrane production mediated new functional synapses. Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9); Ulus et al. (2006) [[10]](#pm-ref-10); Cansev et al. (2005) [[11]](#pm-ref-11); Wurtman et al. (2006) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) #### (Mechanism boundary) This PM concerns physical connection formation, stabilisation, remodelling and elimination. It does not take over transmitter synthesis/signalling, electrophysiological LTP without structural measurement, phosphatidylcholine synthesis, DHA incorporation, neurogenesis or general injury protection. Excitatory spine, inhibitory-marker, presynaptic active-zone and electron-microscopy results retain their measurement identities. Healthy adaptation, development and ageing are distinguished; injury-repair efficacy is not established by this corpus.
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Longitudinal animal imaging supports task-related spine formation and selective retention; sleep experiments add pruning and resizing, including electron-microscopy-confirmed contacts. Local signalling, actin remodelling and developmental microglial engulfment explain distinct steps. Nutrient experiments show membrane-precursor responses and a DHA–UMP spine effect, not verified human synapse growth. Excitatory spine, inhibitory-marker, ultrastructural, protein and behavioural endpoints remain separate. A developmental DHA study adds contact-marker and cortical-function evidence; defined meal scheduling changes regional maintenance under obesogenic exposure. These contexts do not establish ordinary adult-human benefits. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - [BRS1-FM5 — Neuronal Connectivity & Structural Adaptation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm5/brs1-fm5-neuronal-connectivity-and-structural-adaptation) — integrates the structural organisation supporting neuronal communication; this PM provides its initially assessed structural process. ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS2-FM3-PM7 — Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation) — the Kennedy route provides membrane material; precursor tracing is separate from structural plasticity and does not transfer every dietary admission. Ulus et al. (2006) [[10]](#pm-ref-10); Cansev et al. (2005) [[11]](#pm-ref-11); Wurtman et al. (2006) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) - [BRS6-FM2-PM4 — Cortisol Rhythm Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm2/brs6-fm2-pm4-cortisol-rhythm-regulation) — glucocorticoid exposure can alter spine turnover in mice; this does not demonstrate a structural benefit from changing human cortisol timing. Liston and Gan (2011) [[16]](#pm-ref-16) ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation) — DHA delivery and incorporation supply membrane context; this PM separately assesses spine remodelling, rather than treating incorporation as proof of new synapses. Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) - [BRS1-FM4-PM10 — Glutamate Clearance & Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm4/brs1-fm4-pm10-glutamate-clearance-and-recycling) — extracellular transmitter handling affects activity context; it does not own physical connection remodelling. Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) - [BRS1-FM4-PM11 — Excitotoxicity Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm4/brs1-fm4-pm11-excitotoxicity-modulation) — injury protection is distinct from healthy learning-related formation and pruning; the reviewed structural studies do not establish injury repair. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Each Phenome relationship has two independent ratings. They are not combined or averaged.

data.title: SAMe Synthesis
data.mission: Maintain methionine adenosyltransferase capacity to convert methionine and ATP into SAMe, sustaining the methyl-donor pool used by downstream methyltransferases.
data.summary: Methionine adenosyltransferase forms S-adenosylmethionine from methionine and ATP. Magnesium and potassium ions coordinate that ATP-dependent catalysis. This reaction supplies the methyl donor used by many later enzymes. Upstream methionine regeneration and later methyl-transfer reactions remain separate processes. Circulating SAMe and the SAM:SAH ratio describe pool balance rather than synthesis speed.

phenome_relationships.rationale: SAMe supplies methyl groups used by many downstream pathways relevant to neural function, but this is an inferred downstream bridge rather than evidence that MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis itself modulates Cognitive Clarity. The attached methylation review establishes SAMe's donor role, not a cognitive outcome or endogenous synthesis-flux effect {{cite:chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996}}. Circulating SAMe or SAM:SAH measurements cannot isolate MAT synthesis from utilisation and clearance {{cite:corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022}}. Direct relationship evidence remains a gap.

SAMe-dependent methylation is biologically relevant to downstream neurotransmitter and membrane chemistry, but the attached mood-disorder review concerns exogenous SAMe and combined folate/B12 treatment rather than endogenous MAT activity or SAMe synthesis flux {{cite:cicero_combined_2022}}. It therefore does not directly demonstrate that this PM modulates Emotional Regulation; the relationship remains an indirect framework bridge with a direct-evidence gap.
